EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
We exploit two independent sources of quasi-experimental variation in the salience of commodity taxes.

A. Grocery-store field experiment (weekly scanner data)  
 Method: Difference-in-Differences with a triple difference (DDD) robustness check and an event-study visualization.  
 Why: The store introduced highly visible tax-inclusive shelf tags for a subset of taxable products during a clearly dated, short intervention while leaving (i) the same products in two matched stores and (ii) other taxable products in the same store untouched. Absent the new tags, treated and control units face the same statutory 7.375 % sales tax; only salience changes. The staggered timing is trivial (single start date) and the panel is balanced, so 2-way fixed-effects DID is appropriate.

B. State-level beer panel (1970–2003)  
 Method: Two-way fixed-effects panel regression (DID) that compares consumption responses to (log) excise taxes (embedded in posted prices) versus sales taxes (added at the register). Identification comes from within-state changes over time and cross-state heterogeneity in tax type and rate.  
 Why: Excise and sales tax changes are frequent and not mechanically linked. By including state and year FE, we control for all time-invariant state factors and nationwide shocks. A single regression with both taxes isolates how the same population responds to equally sized but differently salient taxes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. Store-level experiment  
 • Treatment variable: Tax salience_dummy = 1 for product-store-week observations in which a tax-inclusive shelf tag is present.  
 • Control groups (two dimensions)  
  1. Within treated store: taxable toiletry items that never received new tags.  
  2. Across stores: the exact same UPCs in two nearby stores that never received new tags.  
 • Timing: Weeks 8–10 of 2006 (inclusive). Pretreatment is week 1 2005 – week 7 2006; post-treatment is week 8 – 13 2006.  
 • Outcome: log(Quantity) and log(Price-inclusive revenue/Quantity).  

B. State-level beer panel  
 • Treatment variables:  
  ExciseTax = log(1 + excise tax per gallon)  
  SalesTax = log(1 + state sales tax rate)  
 • Control: The counterfactual for a tax change in state s is provided by all other states in the same year plus the pre-change years of state s.  
 • Timing: Event = any statutory change; multiple events per state.  
 • Outcome: log(per-capita beer consumption).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends (store-level): In the absence of visible shelf tags, treated UPCs in the treatment store would have followed the same sales path as (i) untreated taxable UPCs in that store and (ii) the same UPCs in control stores.  
 • Plausibility: Same chain, same regional promotions, same tax rate; intervention is purely informational and only three weeks long.  

A2. No other contemporaneous shocks differentially affecting treated products (e.g., promotion, price change, shelf relocation).  
 • Plausibility: Intervention was researcher-initiated; store managers agreed not to run simultaneous promotions. We will verify in the price data.  

B1. Exogeneity of within-state timing of excise vs sales tax changes relative to beer demand shocks.  
 • Plausibility: Alcohol-policy history suggests tax changes are driven by fiscal & political cycles rather than short-run consumption shocks. Inclusion of controls for drinking age, DUI laws, unemployment, income and year FE increases plausibility.  

B2. Stable unit treatment value (no cross-border shopping large enough to bias state-year per-capita consumption).  
 • Plausibility: Beer is bulky and low value-to-weight; literature finds small cross-border effects except for very small states. We will test by dropping border counties & small states.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Promotion/Supply shocks coinciding with shelf-tag weeks  
  • Mitigation: (i) Control for weekly price promotions; (ii) include product*week fixed effects across stores, which net out chain-wide promotions.  

2. Differential seasonality around the three-week window (e.g., Valentine’s Day cosmetics spike)  
  • Mitigation: (i) Include week-of-year fixed effects; (ii) run an event-study ±12 weeks to ensure no pre-trend and symmetry.  

3. Policy endogeneity in beer panel (states raise taxes when consumption is rising/falling)  
  • Mitigation: (i) Two-way FE soak up state trends; (ii) include state-specific linear trends; (iii) placebo test using cigarette consumption; (iv) instrument posted beer prices with statutory taxes when estimating price elasticities to show consistent patterns.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R CODE OUTLINE  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Install/load packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

#----------------------------
# A. Store-level DID
#----------------------------
scanner <- read_csv("scanner_grocery_CA_2005_2006.csv")

# Construct variables
scanner <- scanner %>% 
  mutate(week_id      = as.integer(week),
         post         = if_else(week_id >= 8 & year==2006, 1, 0),
         treat_upc    = if_else(category %in% c("cosmetics","hair accessories","deodorant"),1,0),
         treat_store  = if_else(store_id == "TreatmentStore",1,0),
         salience     = post * treat_upc * treat_store,   # DDD term
         ln_q         = log(quantity + 1),
         ln_revenue   = log(revenue + 1))

# Main DID (two-way FE)
did_res <- feols(ln_q ~ salience + post:treat_upc + post:treat_store + 
                 treat_upc:treat_store | upc_id + week_id + store_id, 
                 data = scanner, cluster = ~store_id)
summary(did_res)

# Event-study
scanner <- scanner %>% 
  mutate(rel_week = week_id - 8)  # 0 = first treatment week
event_res <- feols(ln_q ~ i(rel_week, treat_upc*treat_store, ref = -1) | 
                   upc_id + store_id + week_id, 
                   cluster = ~store_id,
                   data = scanner %>% filter(rel_week>=-12 & rel_week<=12))
iplot(event_res)

# Robustness: drop untreated taxable products
did_cat <- feols(ln_q ~ salience | upc_id + week_id + store_id, 
                 data = scanner %>% filter(category %in% c("cosmetics","hair accessories","deodorant")),
                 cluster = ~store_id)

#----------------------------
# B. State-level panel
#----------------------------
beer <- read_csv("state_beer_1970_2003.csv") %>%
  mutate(ln_beer_pc   = log(beer_pc),
         ln_excise    = log(1 + excise_tax_per_gallon),
         ln_sales     = log(1 + sales_tax_rate),
         ln_income    = log(per_capita_income))

# Main specification
beer_res <- feols(ln_beer_pc ~ ln_excise + ln_sales + drinking_age + dui_law + 
                  ln_income + unemployment | state + year, 
                  cluster = ~state, data = beer)
summary(beer_res)

# Robustness: add state-specific linear trends
beer_trend <- feols(ln_beer_pc ~ ln_excise + ln_sales + drinking_age + dui_law + 
                    ln_income + unemployment | state + year + state[trend], 
                    cluster = ~state, data = beer)
summary(beer_trend)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory (Chetty et al. 2009; Finkelstein 2009) predicts that making taxes more salient increases the elasticity of demand with respect to the after-tax price.  

A. Store-level: Visible tags should reduce quantity by roughly the tax-exclusive price elasticity times the 7.375 % tax. Prior grocery elasticity estimates for toiletries are around −0.8 to −1.2. If salience raises perceived prices fully, we expect a 6–10 % decline in quantity for treated UPCs during the three weeks (coefficient on salience ≈ −0.06 to −0.10 in logs).  

B. State-level: The absolute elasticity with respect to excise taxes should be larger (in magnitude) than for sales taxes. I expect |β_excise| ≈ 0.3–0.5 and |β_sales| ≈ 0.05–0.2, implying about a 2- to 4-fold difference in salience.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)  

C1: Parallel pre-trends verified by event-study ….. 1  
C2: No differential contemporaneous shocks …………. 0.8  
C3: Stable composition / no migration ………………… 1  
C4: Treatment exogeneity (tags not targeted to rising/falling products) ……… 0.9  
C5: No interference / spillovers to controls …………. 0.7  

Average ≈ 0.88 → generally credible but still requires careful robustness checks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This empirical plan leverages both a high-frequency field experiment and 33 years of nationwide panel data to cleanly isolate how the visibility of commodity taxes shapes consumer behavior, tax incidence, and welfare.
